issues.legal_issue: A custodian’s transfer of vested evacuee property is invalid when it is made without the required prior approval and without a process directed at obtaining the best price.
material_facts: The disputed property had vested in the Custodian as evacuee property.
The property was transferred by negotiation to a private purchaser after an earlier auction and related proceedings.
The transfer was made without the Custodian General’s prior approval and without a tender process to secure the best price.
The High Court set aside the transfer order and the resulting sale certificate, and the Supreme Court upheld that decision.
issues.conclusion: The transfer order and the sale certificate were invalid, and the High Court was justified in directing their cancellation.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 8 and 10(1) and (2) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, property vests in the Custodian, whose primary duty is to preserve and maintain it. Transfer or sale is permissible only for the purposes specified in Section 10(1); it requires the Custodian General’s previous approval, not post facto approval. A process such as tender should be used to ensure the best price is obtained.

rule.if: evacuee_property_management_proceeding and property_vested_in_custodian and transfer_made_without_prior_required_approval and no_competitive_price_process

predicates.evacuee_property_management_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the management or transfer of property held by a public custodian as evacuee property.
predicates.property_vested_in_custodian: The property had vested in the custodian responsible for preserving and maintaining it.
predicates.transfer_made_without_prior_required_app: The custodian arranged a transfer without obtaining the required approval before making the transfer order.
predicates.no_competitive_price_process: The property was transferred without a competitive process intended to obtain the best available price.
predicates.custodian_property_transfer_invalid: The transfer of the custodian-held property cannot stand.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns property vested in a custodian, a transfer made without prior required approval and a competitive price process cannot stand.

issues.legal_issue: A public-law order obtained through deliberate deception or concealment of material information that induces an authority to act cannot be allowed to stand.
material_facts: Earlier proceedings and orders concerning the property were not disclosed in the later proceedings.
The later transfer application was made years after the earlier orders, and the Supreme Court found substance in the contention that relevant facts had been suppressed.
The purchaser under the earlier auction was not given an opportunity to be heard before the later transfer order was made.
The Supreme Court considered that fraud appeared to have been practised and upheld the High Court’s decision setting aside the later transfer.
issues.conclusion: The concealment of relevant prior orders and the circumstances surrounding the later transfer supported the conclusion that the transfer orders could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Fraud in public law involves deception or deliberate misrepresentation that induces an authority to exercise power it otherwise would not have exercised; material suppression may amount to fraud on the court. Fraud vitiates proceedings and cannot be preserved by equitable doctrines. The Court relied on State of A.P. v. T. Suryachandra Rao, S.P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath, Ram Chandra Singh v. Savitri Devi, Shrisht Dhawan v. Shaw Brothers, Ram Preeti Yadav v. U.P. Board of High School and Intermediate Education, and Gowrishankar v. Joshi Amba Shankar Family Trust, among other authorities.

predicates.public_law_property_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an authority’s exercise of public power over property.
predicates.material_prior_orders_concealed: A person seeking the authority’s action withheld earlier orders that were material to the application.
predicates.concealment_induced_authority_to_act: The concealment led the authority to take action it would not otherwise have taken.
predicates.fraud_tainted_order_cannot_stand: An order obtained through the material deception cannot remain in force.

issues.definition: If material prior orders are concealed in a public-law property proceeding and that concealment induces official action, the resulting order cannot stand.

issues.legal_issue: An order alleged to be a nullity must still be challenged before it can be treated as having no legal effect.
material_facts: The parties disputed the legal effect and challengeability of earlier orders concerning the property.
The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that an order could simply be disregarded as a nullity, stating that even a null order must be challenged.
The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Gurdev Singh.
issues.conclusion: An order cannot be treated as ineffective merely by asserting that it is a nullity; it must be challenged.
issues.legal_principle: Even an order alleged to be void or a nullity must be challenged; the Court relied on State of Punjab v. Gurdev Singh.

predicates.proceeding_concerning_effect_of_order: The proceeding concerns whether an existing order has legal effect.
predicates.operative_order_alleged_to_be_nullity: A party asserts that an existing order is a nullity.
predicates.alleged_nullity_order_must_be_challenged: The order must be challenged rather than simply disregarded as void.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns the effect of an existing order alleged to be a nullity, that order must be challenged.
